summary:
The statutory baseline in Austria is permissive. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971, marriage equality has applied since 2017, and same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2016. The Equal Treatment Act has covered employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2004, and recent amendments have broadened its use of "gender" to encompass gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics; gender identity and intersex status are not listed separately but are treated as covered under that term. By January 2017 every federal state had extended anti-discrimination protection to goods and services, Lower Austria being the last to do so.

Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1 January 2016, and offences committed on that ground are treated as an aggravating factor in sentencing. The 1993 Security Police Act obliges police to avoid actions that could be perceived as biased on grounds of sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition is possible without mandatory medical procedures. After the Constitutional Court ruled in June 2018 that gender identity must be accurately reflected in official documents, an "X" marker became available on passports and a "divers" entry on birth certificates; the Interior Ministry restricted "divers" to people holding a medical panel certificate of intersexuality, and intersex people may choose "diverse", "inter" or no designation. Changing legal gender and name does not require prior sex-reassignment surgery but is conditional on submitting a psychiatric opinion.

Detention carries a defined framework. A Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report published in 2025, produced within an EU-funded project, sets out the legal rules governing LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons and their situation and rights in detention, including gender self-determination and anti-discrimination protection. The Justice Ministry answered parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 in May and June 2025 on the official rules for housing transgender people in penal institutions; that answer is the authority to cite if a trans visitor is detained, and it is published in German.

Violence risk is documented and recent. In March 2025 police uncovered a neo-Nazi network that used fake dating profiles to lure gay and bisexual men to ambushes by masked assailants, who filmed the attacks and shared them. Austrian police arrested 15 people aged 14 to 26 over a wave of hate attacks in which at least 17 LGBTQ people were lured via fake dating-platform accounts to remote locations, ambushed by masked groups, filmed and falsely accused of being paedophiles; investigators believe the real victim count is much higher. Official figures for 2025 record 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 7,327 prejudice motives, with 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence, and police data acknowledges under-recording. Across the reporting year homophobic offences rose while transphobic incidents declined.

Political conditions are unsettled. The far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) won the most votes in the September 2024 national election, its first such result since the Second World War, on 29.2% of the vote, prompting concern about the consequences of an FPÖ-led government for LGBTQ people. New Ministry of Education rules restrict outside sex-education providers, a Vienna petition for queer sauna time slots was rejected, and the national Ombud has issued guidance on gender-inclusive forms for intersex and non-binary people.

Access to care is supported by professional bodies but partly gated. Puberty blockers for youth experiencing gender dysphoria have been endorsed by the Austrian Society of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and the Austrian Society of Gynecology and Obstetrics, and public health insurance payment for sex-change treatment is bound on submission of psychiatric opinions. Lesbian couples can access artificial insemination and IVF treatments. In 2018 the ultra-conservative association TeenSTAR was found offering minors conversion therapy classes teaching that sexual orientation was changeable; the Education Directorate Salzburg banned TeenSTAR workshops pending review, the association was banned in April 2019, and Parliament passed a resolution on 2 July 2019 calling for a legal ban on conversion therapy on minors, with all parties voting in favour at the final vote.

Open service and public life are established. LGBT people serve openly in the Austrian Armed Forces, and since 2014 transgender people have been allowed to serve openly. Advocacy operates openly through HOSI Wien, founded 1979, HOSI Salzburg, ALGF and Afro Rainbow Austria, with community infrastructure in Vienna, Linz, Innsbruck, Salzburg and Graz and an annual Vienna Gay Pride and Regenbogenparade. Public opinion as of 2023 showed 65% support for same-sex marriage and 66% agreeing nothing is wrong with a same-sex relationship.
tangentialFactors:
Political visibility is high and cuts against the legislative record. Seven National Council politicians were openly gay after the 2019 election, Iris Eliisa Rauskala became the first openly LGBT government minister in June 2019, Georg Djundja became Austria's first openly gay mayor in April 2019, and President Alexander Van der Bellen took part in the 2019 EuroPride parade in Vienna. The ÖVP and FPÖ have historically opposed LGBT rights, and the FPÖ's 2024 result places a party with that record at the head of the polls.

Historical prosecutions remain unaddressed. Lesbianism was criminalised after the Anschluss and courts were aligned to Paragraph 175 in 1940; as of July 2020 no expungement or compensation scheme for historical convictions had been implemented.

The source material notes that many LGBT minorities still regard being different as a problem, a sentiment attributed to Catholic influence, which bears on how the permissive statutory baseline is experienced in practice.

outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources in the inventory, a Graz election item and the Amnesty International Austria report, yielded no substantive Austria-specific finding and contribute nothing to this record.

Whether the conversion-therapy ban called for by the National Council resolution of 2 July 2019 has since been enacted is unresolved in the available material; only the resolution, the April 2019 ban on the association and the Salzburg education ban are sourced.

The currency of the psychiatric-opinion requirement for legal gender change and for insurance coverage of sex-change treatment is not independently dated in the inventory, and the Justice Ministry answer on housing transgender detainees is available only in German.

Police hate-crime data for 2025 is acknowledged by its own reporting to under-record incidents, and the inventory does not break the 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence down by transgender status, so the scale of trans-specific violence relative to homophobic violence is unresolved beyond the direction of travel noted for the reporting year.
